Our performance data is publicly verifiable, with the complete methodology and sources for our purchase invoices provided for reference. We run five different performance tests 24/7, 365 days a year on every host and measure its speed, uptime, traffic handling capacity, server power and worldwide loading speed . We won’t discuss the features and specifications listed on the host’s sales page; instead, we’ll dismantle each claim through our performance tests. DreamHost Web Hosting Launch plan, priced at $2.89/month, offers 25 websites hosted, the lowest per site anywhere on the internet. DreamHost recorded 474ms TTFB, 99.96% uptime, and 147ms load handling response time. Their global TTFB tested from 40 locations stands at 385ms. The performance is not top-notch, they aren’t leaders in any of the performance tests but they stand right at the median center of all 23 hosts. If you are a freelancer or a small agency handling multiple client sites, DreamHost can be a huge bill saver for you. You’ll get a free domain, daily backups and a great control panel. They also claim to offer 100% uptime guarantee but we’re not sure how it works, as our test sites recorded only 99.96% uptime over our 12-month window. Also, it’s not possible to get 100% uptime on a shared host and we say this based on tracking the uptime for the last six years across 36 monitored endpoints. GreenGeeks : GreenGeeks moves from our recommended host to notable mentions. The uptime performance is degrading massively in the last few months while TTFB and load handling is still top notch. We still give a buy call to GreenGeeks but we recommend to go with pro or premium plan instead of Starter plan. It offers the fastest load handling (26ms) of any of the 23 shared web hosts we’ve tested, and its 423ms speed is second only to Bluehost at 412ms. GreenGeeks has been consistently outperforming other hosts in these tests for the last six years and it’s an impressive achievement. It includes everything you expect from a hosting company: free domain, daily backups, email hosting, AI website builder and 24/7 customer support. I especially love how they employ quality Human support via live chat rather than using AI for support. It has data centers in Chicago, Montreal, Amsterdam and Singapore. However, their uptime score of 99.91% with 55 outages adds a little bit of concern for us. In simple terms, for the last 12 months, our test site hosted on GreenGeeks has been down 55 times, which is higher than Hostinger Business with 6 outages and Bluehost with 10 outages. NameCheap : NameCheap offers the lowest renewal price on its plans. We have tested their Stellar plan costs $1.98/month and it renews at $4.88/month, just 2.5x markup increase, the lowest in the industry after InterServer’s 1x. Their performance is decent for a shared host. The TTFB score is 479ms, 99.39% uptime recorded and load handling score of 150ms, measured from November 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026. Page load times hold up well for a shared host, but uptime has slipped sharply across 19 outages, most of them concentrated in May and June 2026. If you’re running a news site or getting regular concurrent visitors, NameCheap will disappoint your visitors. The major drawback: They offer up to two backups every week, but it’s not guaranteed. Sounds weird, right? It means they might or might not take backups for a week. At least, a guaranteed weekly backup will be good instead of this uncertain offering. Backups are one of the most essential things for a web hosting company. In the last six years, our backups saved us numerous times from outages, restoring sites after a crash, etc. Our methodology gives maximum weightage to backups, but NameCheap disappoints us. We usually don’t recommend a host with no reliable backups. NameCheap offers fixed automatic backups in their top tier plans, so if you believe they’re fit for your requirements, try their Stellar Plus and Business plan but Stellar plan is simply not recommended. InMotionHosting: InMotion Hosting is one of the renowned web hosting service providers in the industry, which has been around for more than two decades. The plans are super cheap to get started with a low introductory price. The performance is decent across TTFB, uptime, and load handling. However, they upsell automated backups at $2.99/month, which sustainably increases the overall hosting costs. They also don’t include Email hosting and come as an add-on $3/month. In comparison, our top recommended hosts like GreenGeeks and HostArmada come with everything included, still priced affordably and offering faster performance than InMotionHosting. Since we didn’t have any dealbreakers, we are skipping them in our top recommendations. Cloudways: Cloudways is one of the industry’s first managed cloud hosting providers. It offers you to host your site across five different cloud providers like DigitalOcean, Linode, Vultr, Google Cloud, and Amazon Web Services. We have tested three popular providers like DigitalOcean, Vultr, and Linode. Our data shows their load handling performance has degraded in the last three months with the services getting unresponsive after 30 seconds and struggles to handle load. However, they are much superior in TTFB and uptime performance. Their uptime has been clocking 99.9% to 100% consistently every month for the last six years. Their TTFB response time sits inside the top five of the 23 hosts we track. If you are looking for a hosting where load handling does not matter and need to host unlimited sites with no increased renewal prices, Cloudways could be your choice. HostGator: Both HostGator and Bluehost come under a single parent company called “NewFold Digital Inc.”. We noticed the company has upgraded HostGator data centers to Oracle Cloud, much like Bluehost. Both of them carry the same dashboard, same backend support team and similar pricing. However, when any of the new features are getting deployed, we see them first at Bluehost rather than HostGator. For example, they introduced the Cloudflare CDN integrated within their dashboard. We saw this feature first at Bluehost, and after some months of testing, we saw it on the HostGator dashboard. There is nothing particularly unique to HostGator, and we are already recommending Bluehost. Companies We Tested but Do Not Recommend: FastComet : FastComet is yet another shared web hosting that works much like GreenGeeks, Hostinger, etc. However, they were acquired by Hosting.com a few months back. After the acquisition, Hosting.com is removing the existing data centers powered by FastComet, and the sites are getting moved to Hosting.com’s data center. So even though they look like a separate brand, both the FastComet and Hosting.com’s website will be hosted in the same server infrastructure. We are also not sure whether FastComet as a brand will be continued separately or whether it will be merged with Hosting.com. Since our six years of performance data we have collected is based on FastComet’s old data center. Since we are moving to Hosting.com’s new data center, which is not reliable based on our existing performance data, we are not recommending them currently. SiteGround : SiteGround is one of the most popular hosting companies in the industry. However, the performance has been degrading year over year. When we started testing in 2020, the performance was top-notch. However, as time passes, we see very much declining performance, particularly in uptime. The outages are pretty consistent across months, and we sense the reason could be overloading their servers beyond the limit or poor technical architecture. The only good thing is their load handling which has been consistent at ~150 – 170ms across all these years. ChemiCloud : ChemiCloud has been consistently performing below average across years. We noted their starter plan is restricted with very low server resources causing consistent outages. They have moved multiple infrastructure upgrades over the years but nothing improved their services. We also had like a 6 hour long outage due to issues with their infrastructure partners. Ionos: Ionos is a below average performer over our 12-month window. Their TTFB stands at 527ms, uptime at 99.94% and the load handling fails. Their global TTFB sits at 480ms. On top of that, it took us a few months to completely understand their dashboard. Even after nearly using it for a year, I can’t confidently hangout and do our work. NameHero : We have started testing NameHero in 2022. Initially the performance was decent across all the performance metrics. However, as the time grows, we are experiencing outages every single day. Their uptime over our 12-month window is 99.89%, across 104 separate outages, which is pretty concerning and it’s also their guaranteed uptime SLA. GoDaddy: GoDaddy is one of the slowest web hosting providers in the industry. They have scored worst in uptime at 99.76%, measured from November 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026, and their load handling fails as their servers are unable to handle our simple load test. Both the US and global TTFB scores are poor to the core. We would never recommend them for any kind of site. Contrary, Godaddy Managed hosting is faster and runs completely on a different server architecture. Interserver : We have started testing Interserver in Q4 2025 and it started off exceptionally well. It was the number one ranked host in our Q4 2025 web hosting rankings. However, as time progressed, the performance got degraded with a large outage of 5+ hours happening in a single day. At least once a month, we are getting this 5+ half of downtime, and as a result, their average uptime from November 1, 2025 to October 31, 2026 is 99.71%, which is below the uptime SLA. We really liked the concept of same renewal price at $2.50 per month, however the uptime made it worse to host our sites there. Our Verdict The Web hosting needs differ based on various factors like geographical location, type of audience, type of sites, etc. We try to consolidate most of the factors and recommend you selected three hosts out of the seven hosts which we are recommending above. If you are looking for the best overall hosting provider, choose Bluehost . It ticks all the boxes like performance, pricing, support and value for money. At $1.99/month, getting an oracle cloud infrastrucure with 99.99% uptime SLA is great to host any kind of websites. It also offers faster global speed, thanks to its inbuilt CDN. The support is human powered and no AI involved which is actually less hassles, solves the problem directly instead of going through AI route where unsolved queries requires additional human support adding hassles for website owners who want their issues to be fixed as soon as possible. The dashboard is much matured with easy navigation for all features. If you are looking to host multiple sites that require top-notch performance, then choose Hostinger . It includes everything from daily backups, SSL, CDN, and their email hosting alone comes as an add-on. You can host at least 3 websites on the starter plan and up to 25 websites on the business plan. Read the Full Cloudways Review → 7. DigitalOcean: best unmanaged VPS for developers Best for: developers who want a whole server to themselves and are comfortable on the command line. Backups add 20% of the Droplet price for weekly or 30% for daily, and free support is ticket-based, with replies in under 24 hours. An uptime promise sets the payout for downtime. It doesn’t measure how often a site goes down, which is why we list what our own monitoring recorded. Other hosts we considered These hosts have HostingGuider reviews but missed this list. Each can still be right for one specific need. GoDaddy: Economy puts one site, daily backups, and email on a single plan. At $5.99 a month for three years, then $11.99, it costs more per site than Hostinger or Bluehost. HostGator: Hatchling covers 10 sites, but it renews at $10.99 to $17.59 a month , keeps one week of courtesy backups, and won’t let you choose a data center. IONOS: good long-term shared value, with daily backups kept 14 days and a free personal consultant. Its intro prices last only one year. InterServer: renews at a steady $7 a month on any term, which suits people who hate price jumps. It isn’t the cheapest in the first years. HostArmada: one site on a budget with stated CPU and RAM, plus a 45-day money-back window on shared plans. Which type of web hosting do you need? Most first websites need shared hosting. Move up only when traffic, budget, or skills call for it. Shared hosting: your site shares a server with others. It’s the cheapest and easiest type. Hostinger, SiteGround, Namecheap, and Bluehost sell it. Managed WordPress hosting: the host tunes the server for WordPress and handles updates, security, and backups. Kinsta is our pick. Managed cloud hosting: you get dedicated cloud resources and the host runs the server. Cloudways fits here, and so does Hostinger Cloud Startup. VPS hosting: you get your own virtual server and full control. DigitalOcean is our developer pick. Each type is laid out side by side in how the main hosting types differ . Which web host should you choose? Starting your first blog or portfolio? Hostinger Premium: the lowest four-year cost, plus two spare sites for side projects. Business site where a lost day of edits hurts? SiteGround. In our view, 30 days of daily backups and phone access justify the higher bill. Don’t want to pay years upfront? Namecheap Stellar or Stellar Plus, billed yearly or monthly. Running five to ten small sites? Bluehost Starter, which covers 10. Your WordPress site makes money and you want it managed? Kinsta. An agency hosting client sites? Cloudways, so many sites can share one server. A developer who wants root access? DigitalOcean. Most readers end up choosing between the first two. Compare Hostinger’s 48-month deal with SiteGround’s backup-heavy plans and pick the one that matches your site type. Frequently asked questions What is web hosting? Web hosting is rented space on a server that stores your website’s files and serves them to visitors. Without it, your domain name has nothing to point to. What is the best web hosting for beginners? Hostinger suits most beginners. Premium costs $143.52 for four years, includes a first-year domain, and lets you choose from 12 server locations. How much does web hosting cost? A small site on shared hosting costs about $2 to $18 a month, depending on the plan and term. Managed cloud and managed WordPress plans on this list start at $11 and $35 a month. The renewal rate is the number to watch, because it can be three to six times the intro price. Hostinger Premium goes from $2.99 to $10.99 a month. Seasonal sales lower the first term further, so check the Black Friday hosting discounts before paying the regular intro price. Do I need to buy my domain from my web host? No. You can register a domain anywhere and point it at your host. Buying both together is simpler, and Hostinger, Bluehost, and IONOS include a free domain for the first year. Keeping them apart means a hosting dispute can’t hold up your domain. Is it better to choose a local or global web host? Pick a host with a data center near your visitors, wherever the company is based. Our Singapore server replied more than four times faster from Singapore than from Sydney: 157 ms against 674 ms. Is free web hosting worth it? Not for a site you care about. Paid shared hosting starts at a few dollars a month and adds your own domain, backups, and support. Can I switch web hosts later? Yes. You can move a site to a new host at any time, which is one reason not to prepay longer than you’re sure about. Kinsta includes unlimited free migrations. How we compared web hosting providers We compared only providers that HostingGuider reviews in full, using official pricing, refund, backup, and data center pages read in late September 2026. Four paid accounts supply the first-hand numbers: two Hostinger plans (Business Web Hosting and Cloud Startup), Namecheap Stellar Plus, and Kinsta WP 2. For SiteGround, Bluehost, Cloudways, and DigitalOcean, we relied on published terms. We’ll add our own numbers if we buy those plans. The ranking reflects fit by need and four-year cost. text: Entry plans in shared hosting renew at two to six times what they advertise, with SiteGround’s StartUp going from $2.99 to $17.99 and Namecheap’s Stellar from $2.28 to $4.66. A few dollars a month still buys a working product, though the low tier buys it alongside a published set of ceilings on files, CPU seconds, backup frequency and support, all of them readable before purchase. Both numbers, the one on the ad and the one on the renewal notice, appear on a host’s own pages. Topic Key Point Renewal pricing The advertised number is what the first invoice costs What gets cut Four published ceilings, all readable before purchase Three-year math The ranking changes depending on the year measured GreenGeeks Top pick, LiteSpeed on NVMe with daily backups included Hostinger Lowest four-year cost on a 48-month prepay InterServer One plan at $7, locked for the life of the account DreamHost Monthly billing on every plan, renewal printed on the card ChemiCloud Publishes cores, RAM and inodes on the pricing table InMotion Hosting 100 GB at the entry tier, backups sold separately SiteGround Support-led pick with the steepest renewal step here Krystal UK and EU, publishes processes and cores openly Bluehost and HostGator Biggest brands, hardest ownership questions Community picks The curated lists disagree with the affiliate lists The verdict Which of the two numbers the buyer pays The Gap Between Intro Price and Renewal Price Almost every mainstream budget host discounts the first term by between 60% and 83%. The advertised price is customer acquisition cost, and the regular price is what the product costs to run. That discount applies to the first invoice and to nothing after it. The Intro-to-Renewal Spread in 2026 Host Entry plan Intro Renewal Multiple SiteGround StartUp $2.99 $17.99 6.0x ChemiCloud Starter $2.49 $11.95 4.8x GreenGeeks Lite $2.95 $13.95 4.7x ScalaHosting Mini $2.95 $11.95 4.0x InMotion Core (1yr) $2.99 $11.99 4.0x DreamHost Launch $2.89 $10.99 3.8x Hostinger Premium (48mo) $2.99 $10.99 3.7x HostGator Hatchling ~$3.75 $10.99 ~2.9x InterServer Standard $2.50 (1 month) $7.00 flat after month one Bluehost Starter (36mo) $3.99 $9.99 2.5x Namecheap Stellar $2.28 $4.66 2.1x IONOS Essential $4.00 $8.00 2.0x The multiples are the least useful column in that table, because the headline almost always requires the longest term paid upfront in full, so Hostinger’s $2.99 is a 48-month commitment billed at $143.52 on the day of signup, and HostGator bills the whole three-year Hatchling term at signup, a total of $395.61 once the renewal rate applies. A low multiple is also not automatically a low price. IONOS’s 2.0x is the result of a smaller discount on a product that was never cheap, while Namecheap’s 2.1x comes with the cheapest renewal in the table at $4.66. Only there does a small multiple mean what a buyer hopes it means. Hostwinds is outside the table for a different reason. Its $4.54 intro against a $6.99 renewal is the smallest step anyone here offers, a genuine point in its favor. InterServer is the one row where the multiple column stops meaning anything. Its $7 rate comes with no term discount to chase. What Is Pushing Regular Hosting Prices Up The supply side explains more of this than greed does. cPanel raised every license tier again on January 1, 2026: Solo from $16 to $18 Admin from $19.75 to $21 Pro from $27.25 to $32 Premier from $47 to $49.50 That is the seventh consecutive annual increase since cPanel moved to per-account pricing in 2019, and combined cost is up more than 55% across most tiers, so a provider running 20 servers on the Pro tier now pays over $640 a month in control-panel licensing before a single customer exists. Plesk announced an average 26% increase for the same January. Hostinger’s hPanel, ScalaHosting’s SPanel, InterServer’s DirectAdmin and DreamHost’s custom panel each remove a per-account license fee from the cost floor. Hosts that do not run cPanel price flatter for it, and their renewal numbers are lower. What Gets Cut on a $3 Hosting Plan The four ceilings below are where the $2.95 comes from. Three of them have a published number the buyer can look up before checkout, and the fourth does not. Inode Limits An inode is one file. Every folder counts, and so does every separate email message held in a mailbox. A bare WordPress install therefore sits at roughly 20,000 to 25,000 files before a single page is published. Most published entry-tier numbers are between 200,000 and 300,000, and the interesting cases are the two hosts whose published number is not the one they enforce. HostGator sets a 100,000 soft limit above which the account silently drops out of weekly backups, applies a 20 GB size threshold that does the same thing, and treats 200,000 as a policy violation. Bluehost publishes 50,000 while its own knowledge base says it usually takes no action below 1,000,000. GreenGeeks enforces an inode quota and surfaces it in cPanel as File Usage, sending a graduated resource alert before acting, though it publishes no per-plan figure. InterServer, ScalaHosting, Hostwinds and InMotion publish no inode number either, which leaves the ceiling in place and out of view. CPU, RAM and Entry Processes A cheap plan that passes this second ceiling slows down, and outright failure is the rarer outcome, though each host measures the allowance in its own units, so the comparison is difficult before any number is read. The two ends of the practice: SiteGround meters CPU seconds rather than percentages, at 1,000 an hour and 300,000 a month on its entry plan. HostGator caps a percentage instead, at 25% CPU with 25 simultaneous processes and 25 concurrent MySQL connections. No two hosts here measure the same thing. Comparing CPU allowances across a shortlist produces nothing usable. ScalaHosting publishes a per-account ceiling of 3% on Mini in its terms of service, while Bluehost, InMotion, InterServer and Hostwinds publish nothing here at all. An account at its process limit returns HTTP 508, and an account past the plan’s wider limits returns 503, neither of which tells the visitor what happened. Backup Frequency and Retention The roster splits close to evenly between hosts that include a daily copy at the entry tier and hosts that do not. Daily at the entry tier: GreenGeeks, ChemiCloud, DreamHost, IONOS, Krystal and SiteGround. Weekly at the entry tier: InterServer, Hostinger’s Premium tier, Bluehost and HostGator. Neither, without paying: InMotion sells backups as an add-on, and Namecheap Stellar states only that internal backups are ideally performed twice a week though not guaranteed. HostGator’s weekly rotation is conditional in the way described above. Hostwinds, separately, advertises nightly backups on its marketing page while its terms of service state it takes no backups of any kind. Support Support is the one ceiling with no published number, so a buyer cannot verify it before purchase the way an inode cap or a backup schedule can be verified. It costs labor above all, so it tiers with price, and offshoring is the standard way of reducing it. That unverifiable quality is also why some buyers accept the highest renewal price here and treat the renewal step as what the support desk costs. Cheapest Headline or Cheapest Three Years? The three-year arithmetic changes the ranking. GreenGeeks Lite over three years is $35.40 for year one plus $334.80 for years two and three, so $370.20. SiteGround StartUp on the same structure is $35.88 plus $431.76, so $467.64. InterServer is $2.50 plus 35 months at $7, so $247.50. Bluehost Starter on a 36-month prepay is $143.64 for the whole three years before the renewal rate begins. Only two of those four totals came from the two cheapest headline prices, so the year being optimized for decides the winner before any feature comparison starts. GreenGeeks, Best Cheap Web Hosting Overall GreenGeeks is the top pick because of the stack underneath its entry tier. Lite, the entry tier of its shared hosting plans, runs LiteSpeed Enterprise with LSCache on NVMe SSD in RAID-10, with PHP 8.4, HTTP/3 over QUIC and a free Cloudflare CDN. It is $2.95 a month prepaid for 12 months and renews at $13.95, a 4.7x step that sits mid-table. Server-level caching is the difference between a traffic burst reaching PHP and being answered before it gets there, and it shows up in testing. An April 2026 load test at 50,000 visitors recorded a 26 ms response time at 100 concurrent users with zero errors, alongside a 418 ms TTFB in the same run. Any single TTFB number deserves caution, because 2026 testing moves the same host by an order of magnitude depending on test location, concurrency and the state of the CDN. Independent monitoring across 2024 and 2025 logged 99.98% uptime against a 99.9% guarantee. Lite includes 25 GB of storage, unmetered traffic, daily backups, free website transfer handled by the support team, free SSL, 24/7 support and a 30-day money-back window. Two of those, daily backups and hands-on migration, are paid add-ons or DIY plugins at several of the hosts here. Against that, GreenGeeks publishes no per-plan inode figure, and Lite is a single-site plan, so a second site means the Pro tier at $4.95 renewing at $18.95. Since 2009 GreenGeeks has matched three times its hosting energy use in wind credits through the Bonneville Environmental Foundation, none of which changes what the invoice says. Hostinger, Lowest Four-Year Cost Hostinger Premium is $2.99 a month on a 48-month prepay, billed as $143.52 at checkout against a regular price of $575.52. The rate afterward is $10.99 a month. Nothing else here comes near that total four-year outlay, and nothing else asks for four years to reach its headline either. That requirement is the whole of the case against it. Practitioner criticism centers on VPS overselling and on support escalation past the intro window. It publishes the most complete resource table of any host here, down to I/O throughput in KB/s and PHP worker counts per tier, though the documentation around it has not kept up, since the knowledge base still uses older plan names and caps Web Business at 50 websites while the sales page markets unlimited. Running hPanel in place of cPanel removes the license fee from its cost floor, a structural reason its renewal is lower than most competing plans. InterServer, $7 a Month Forever Storage, transfer, websites and databases are all unlimited under a fair-use policy that says the plan is for websites and email, not file storage or reselling. The stack is LiteSpeed with LSCache on CloudLinux behind DirectAdmin, with no cPanel anywhere in it, and the team does the migration itself, including cleanup of problems found on the way. InterServer publishes no inode, CPU or process figures anywhere and argues openly against fixed limits, which suits a buyer who wants one predictable number and leaves nothing to check for a buyer who needs the ceiling in advance. The pricing is one plan at $2.50 for the first month and then $7 a month for as long as the account stays open, with no term discount, since 12 months costs exactly 12 times $7. The Price Lock Guarantee holds that $7 rate for the life of the account, and it holds the standard rate only, narrower than the way the guarantee is usually described. DreamHost, Best for Monthly Billing DreamHost’s case is a billing policy, and monthly billing is available on every plan without forcing a long term. The exact renewal rate is printed next to the promotional price on every plan card. In a market where the renewal number is the last thing a buyer locates, that lets the second year be priced before checkout. Web Hosting Launch is $2.89 a month for the first year and renews at $10.99, with 25 GB of NVMe storage, 25 websites, daily automated backups, unmetered bandwidth, a 100% uptime guarantee and its own control panel in place of cPanel. Support is in-house, and it is also the recurring complaint, alongside a $10.99 to $12.99 standing rate above the cheapest options, with some departing customers reporting that shared support failed to resolve persistent problems. ChemiCloud, the Most Transparent Limits ChemiCloud prints one AMD EPYC core at 3.7 GHz, 2 GB of RAM and 250,000 inodes on the Starter card itself. Almost nobody at this price publishes that much. Starter is $2.49 introductory against an $11.95 regular price on a default 36-month cycle, and it gives 20 GB of NVMe and one website. Daily offsite backups are included with 10 days of retention on Starter, though one-click restore is listed from the Pro tier up and does not appear on the Starter card at all, which is the line the buyer has to read before committing. Email is free and unlimited with MailChannels delivery, and moving an existing site over costs nothing, email included. The money-back window is 45 days against the 30 days most hosts here offer. InMotion Hosting Gives 100 GB at the Entry Tier Core gives 100 GB of storage at the entry tier, four to ten times what most entry plans here provide, though it is plain SSD where the tiers above it are NVMe. The price is $2.99 a month on a one-year term renewing at $11.99, or $3.19 on two and three years renewing at $10.99. It runs NGINX with its own tuning plus cPanel, and says openly that it chose NGINX over LiteSpeed to avoid license costs. It owns its hardware in Los Angeles, Ashburn and Amsterdam, has been independent for 25 years, and offers the longest refund window here at up to 90 days. There is no managed daily backup on shared plans, and Backup Manager is an add-on from $2.99 a month, a serious omission on a plan with 100 GB of space to fill. The storage is still the reason to take Core, since a media library that would fill a 10 GB plan in its first year never comes near that ceiling. SiteGround, Strong Support at the Highest Renewal SiteGround StartUp is $2.99 for the first invoice and $17.99 afterward, the largest spread in this roster at 6.0x. It buys 10 GB of storage, one website and guidance of around 10,000 monthly visits, on Google Cloud infrastructure with 11 hosting regions and more than 170 CDN edge locations. SiteGround publishes unusually specific ceilings, at 200,000 inodes as a hard limit, 768 MB of RAM per process and a 30-minute minimum cron interval, on top of the CPU-second metering described earlier. Up to 30 daily backup copies are included on every shared plan with free restores, better than any other entry plan covered here. Performance testing on SiteGround in 2026 produces inconsistent results, with one test recording a 32 ms TTFB and others putting it between 230 ms and 286 ms, a wider spread than the difference between most hosts here. The renewal is contested among the people paying it. One customer posted a GoGeek auto-renewal of £604 across 13 low-traffic sites and negotiated it down to £403, and the counter-position from operators managing SiteGround accounts by the hundred is that a $7 to $8 monthly difference is minor against hosting that rarely needs a support ticket at all. Krystal for UK and EU Hosting Amethyst is £7 a month monthly, £5.83 on annual and £5.25 on biennial, quoted before VAT, and the pricing page shows no intro-and-renewal split anywhere, unusual enough to be the headline feature. The same page lists 250,000 inodes, 25 processes, one CPU core and 2 GB of RAM. What the page does not do is commit in writing to holding the rate, so the absence of a renewal notice is not the same as a published guarantee of parity. The stack is LiteSpeed with LSCache on CloudLinux behind a mod_security firewall. Backups are daily snapshots, the uptime guarantee is 99.99%, and the money-back window is 60 days. Data centers are in East London, Phoenix, Edison and Amsterdam, all ISO 27001 and on renewable power. Bluehost and HostGator, and Why They Still Rank Bluehost and HostGator are the two most-searched names in budget hosting and both are Newfold brands. Ownership therefore matters here more than either spec sheet does. Bluehost is one of only three hosts officially recommended on WordPress.org, and Newfold is migrating it to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure during 2026. Starter is $3.99 on a 36-month prepay and renews at $9.99 on that term, which is mid-table, though backups are weekly unless CodeGuard is bought separately, free mailbox storage on Starter stops at 100 MB, and the free migration is a DIY plugin. HostGator Hatchling renews at $10.99 on a three-year term, billed as $395.61 upfront, and its published caps are among the most specific of any host here even though its inode policy is among the strictest. During 2026 it began moving customers onto paid cPanel Email tiers priced by active mailbox count, with accounts holding 7 mailboxes and under 50 MB of mail in total moved to a $35.88 annual tier. The ownership question matters most on a three-year prepay. Moody’s downgraded Newfold to Caa1 in February 2025 and Caa3 in September 2025, and the company closed $100 million of new financing in December 2025 and sold MarkMonitor for around $450 million at the end of that year. None of that means the hosting stops working, though it does mean the balance sheet is a live consideration on a long prepay. Ownership changed elsewhere in budget hosting too. HostPapa completed its acquisition of Hostwinds in April 2026, while IONOS answers the staying-power question differently again as a publicly listed operator running US hosting from its own Kansas facility. What the Hosting Community Recommends The curated community lists and the affiliate lists do not agree, and the distance between them is wide enough to matter before either one is trusted. The r/webhosting moderators publish a recommendation thread built from hosts the mod team has personally used, last updated in July 2026. Its US picks are NixiHost, KnownHost and InMotion Hosting, with Zume and Krystal for the UK and EU, on stated criteria of no hidden fees, published renewal rates, in-house support and financial staying power. That thread recommends against relying on mega-brands with very low intro pricing, and names HostGator, SiteGround and Bluehost specifically, while GreenGeeks does not appear on the list at all. Elsewhere in the same forum GreenGeeks comes up in a narrower role, named in a 2026 thread on HostGator’s email repricing as a cPanel-based alternative with free migration and with the first-year discount flagged as a caveat, and named again on a thread about SiteGround alternatives alongside NameHero. That is a narrower endorsement than a list placement, and it arrives with the renewal caveat attached. The other consistent community position is structural, built on keeping off-provider backups, prepaying no more than the buyer can afford to lose, and expecting prices to rise at any host. Knowing how to move a WordPress site without help is what makes that advice usable. Is a Few Dollars a Month Too Good to Be True? No, provided the buyer prices the second number. Four figures settle it before a card is entered, and only one of them is the advertised rate. The renewal figure multiplied by 24 gives the cost of years two and three, and the inode ceiling alongside the backup frequency covers the two limits a small site meets first. The fourth is the refund window, which runs from 72 hours at Hostwinds to 90 days at InMotion. By that test ChemiCloud and Krystal are the most forthcoming hosts here, with GreenGeeks covering three of the four and pointing to File Usage in cPanel for the fourth. Where none of the four appear on a host’s own pages, the buyer finds out what the plan allows only after the account is running and the second invoice has arrived. Frequently Asked Questions How much should web hosting cost per month? Entry shared plans advertise between $2.28 and $4.00 a month in 2026 and renew between $4.66 and $17.99. Budget for the renewal figure, since it is what you pay every year after the first. Why does web hosting cost more when it renews? The advertised price is a first-invoice discount of roughly 60% to 83% used to acquire the customer, and the regular price is what the product costs. Supplier costs are also rising, with cPanel raising license tiers for the seventh consecutive year in January 2026. What is an inode limit in web hosting? An inode is a single file, folder or email message, and hosts cap how many of them an account may hold. A WordPress install uses roughly 20,000 to 25,000 before you add any content. What does “unlimited” web hosting really cover? Unmetered under a fair-use policy. InterServer states plainly that its unlimited plan is for websites and email rather than backup storage or reselling, and Namecheap’s unmetered disk is bound by its acceptable use policy. Do I have to pay for a whole year of hosting upfront? For the advertised price, usually yes, and often longer than a year. Hostinger’s $2.99 rate requires a 48-month prepay of $143.52 and HostGator bills the full term at signup. DreamHost is the notable exception, with monthly billing on every plan. Are backups included with cheap web hosting? It varies more than any other feature. Daily backups are included at the entry tier on GreenGeeks, ChemiCloud, DreamHost, IONOS and Krystal. Bluehost, HostGator, InterServer and Hostinger Premium are weekly, and InMotion sells backups as a $2.99 add-on. Is free website migration really free? At most hosts here it is free and done by their own team, GreenGeeks, InterServer, InMotion and HostGator among them. Bluehost’s free migration is a DIY WordPress plugin, and IONOS sells migration as a paid service. What happened to A2 Hosting? The brand no longer exists. World Host Group acquired A2 Hosting in January 2025 and rebranded it to Hosting.com in April 2025, and a2hosting.com now redirects there. Who owns Bluehost and HostGator? Both are Newfold brands, owned by Clearlake Capital and Siris Capital. Moody’s downgraded Newfold to Caa1 in February 2025 and Caa3 in September 2025. Can I avoid the renewal price by opening a new hosting account? It breaches most hosts’ terms. ScalaHosting goes further and reserves the right to refuse a new package for the same domain for 12 months if a customer declines to renew at the standard price. Is the free domain with a hosting plan really free? For the first year only, and hosts deduct its regular cost from any refund. HostGator deducts $15.00 to $17.99 and Bluehost deducts $15.99, and ChemiCloud only includes a free domain on 36-month plans. Should I choose the cheapest hosting or the cheapest three-year cost? Decide which one you are optimizing for first, because they are different hosts. Over 36 months InterServer costs about $247.50, while a $2.99 headline on a 6.0x renewal reaches roughly $467.64.
